title: Developers Reporting Double-Digit Weekly Time Savings From AI Fell From 68% to 26%
summary:
Atlassian’s State of Developer Experience 2026 finds the share of developers saving ten or more hours a week with AI dropped from 68% to 26% year over year, while only 28% report noticeably less friction than before AI. Engineering leaders report spending more time managing and correcting AI output than developers do.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
summary: Serving web queries at scale with multi-agent systems requires jointly configuring large language models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills. However, the resulting configuration space grows combinatorially, while sparse execution rewards provide limited fine-grained supervision for interdependent planning decisions. We propose EvoRouter, a self-evolving multi-agent routing framework driven by insight-guided on-policy distillation. A dedicated expert periodically synthesizes performance-cost feedback from configuration trajectories across tasks into reusable conditional routing insights about capability requirements, returns from resource scaling, and interactions among configuration choices. A privileged teacher combines these evolving insights with current execution feedback to provide dense token-level supervision for the router's own planning trajectories through on-policy distillation. Cost-aware reinforcement learning jointly optimizes task performance and computational cost. Together, these training signals internalize execution insights into the routing policy. The updated policy generates new trajectories that support subsequent insight extraction, forming an execution-driven self-improvement loop. We evaluate EvoRouter on 19 in-domain datasets spanning five domains and two out-of-domain benchmarks. EvoRouter achieves an average in-domain accuracy of 68.69%, outperforming the strongest routing baseline by 7.23 percentage points while reducing inference compute cost by 50.95%. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/CenYangtze/EvoRouter.

title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

title: Hierarchical Skill Evolution for Coding Agent
summary: Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entangled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progressively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. HSE first extracts task-level evidence from individual trajectories, then aggregates recurring evidence within the same repository to form repository-specific skill candidates, and finally consolidates consistent patterns across repositories into transferable skills across repositories. The evolution is driven by an external writer-evaluator loop that generates and assesses skills while keeping the underlying coding model frozen. The loop externally updates the writer and evaluator policies to improve subsequent skill generation and assessment. This hierarchy progressively filters task-specific details while preserving procedures that generalize across diverse coding environments. Successful trajectories yield reusable guidance for future tasks, while failed trajectories reveal recurring failure modes that guide avoidance and recovery. We evaluate HSE on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE, using GLM-5.2 across Pi and Claude Code harnesses and GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with Pi. Across both benchmarks, 10 skills evolved solely from SWE-Gym improve coding performance across all evaluated settings, demonstrating transfer across benchmarks, coding models, and agent harnesses. We further evolve the skill library from target-benchmark trajectories without verifier feedback, relying solely on the learned evaluator for candidate assessment and achieving additional gains through benchmark-tailored skills.

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. title: Silent and Costly: Characterizing and Detecting Prompt-Caching Mis-Integration in LLM Agents
summary:
Large language model (LLM) services process massive volumes of user requests, resulting in substantial inference costs. To reduce both cost and latency, providers have introduced prompt caching. However, correctly integrating prompt caching is non-trivial due to heterogeneous provider-specific APIs and continuously evolving caching semantics. To understand prompt-caching mis-integration in downstream applications, we conduct the first empirical study of 120 prompt-caching-related pull requests from 10 popular open-source agent systems. Our findings show that prompt-caching mis-integrations arise in both request-side misconfiguration and read-side usage miscount. More importantly, most mis-integrations fail silently without causing observable runtime failures.
  Motivated by these findings, we design CACHELINT, which models a prompt-caching mis-integration as an invocation site together with the preconditions required for correct cache integration. CACHELINT locates caching invocation sites with CodeQL and discharges each precondition either against a dated provider capability oracle or with an LLM guard check. CACHELINT achieves 0.71 precision and 0.78 recall in identifying the 120 labeled mis-integrations across the 10 studied agent systems. Our evaluation further demonstrates the effectiveness of CACHELINT in real-world settings, identifying 32 mis-integrations across 571 agent projects with 0.86 precision. These findings have received 21 developer confirmations and led to 18 upstream fixes, including one in Anthropic's official SDK.

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide reliable external knowledge for multi-hop factual reasoning with large language models (LLMs), yet most KGs in real-world domains such as finance and industry lack question--answer (QA) annotations. Without such annotations, existing methods struggle to improve LLM graph reasoning: training-free agents cannot improve their exploration through interaction; reinforcement learning (RL) agents depend on QA data annotated by humans or synthesized by closed-source models; and training data is typically built offline, so its topology mix is fixed and cannot follow the agent's ability. We propose Evolve on Graph (EoG), a framework that lets an LLM self-evolve its graph reasoning without any QA annotations. Through Graph Self-Play, a single LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. To make questions verifiable, Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) samples reasoning topologies on the KG and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, yielding topology skeletons with correct and complete answer sets; guided by a skeleton, the Proposer explores the graph to pose a multi-hop question. To let task topologies follow the Solver, a Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum rewards the Proposer by the Solver's score variance, keeping questions at the Solver's capability boundary so that complex topologies enter training as the Solver improves. On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata, and an industrial KG, EoG consistently outperforms prompting-, retrieval-, and agent-based methods, showing that LLM graph reasoning can improve through self-play without QA annotations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Szy5/EoG

title: The five components of building a "company harness"
summary: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work.
story_key: story|title:the five components of building a company harness
content_excerpt: We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! All three of our agents can write and execute code, and often need to in order to accomplish tasks. title: Amazon’s Trainium Takes a Strike at the Training King
summary: Trainium Best for Inference? But now good for Training too, Native Trainium PyTorch, High Quality CI, TorchTitan, GPU Impossible Profiler
story_key: story|title:amazon s trainium takes a strike at the training king
content_excerpt: Trainium has already proven itself in the realm of inference. Anthropic is running production inference and RL rollouts on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Historically, Trainium has been great for inference but not the best fit for research training. In inference, the model architecture changes at a much slower pace compared to training, where researchers iterate on many different experiments and ablations of model architecture and need a stack that covers a broad API surface. In the past, that is where Trainium fell short. The AWS Neuron team is aggressively working to change this pitfall with the biggest shift being moving towards a first-class, native PyTorch training experience. Gone are the days of sprinkling xm.step() through your training loop and wrestling with a bespoke XLA-style execution model. Trainium now runs PyTorch the way PyTorch users expect, in eager mode, with torch.compile and the standard APIs. The SemiAnalysis engineering team has been trying out the Trainium3 racks for the past couple of weeks and has found the experience to be great – we love the overall direction of where it is heading. To be clear, it isn’t perfect yet, and we have personally run into a couple of bugs ourselves. It’s nowhere close to the maturity of the CUDA ecosystem, but the direction is right. Their team is making rapid progress with the help of agentic coding. Furthermore, unlike other accelerator companies, where we had to fight tooth and nail to get their engineers a reasonably stable CI fleet, Trainium uses up to 80,000 physical cores allocated towards automated quality control. In this article, we walk through our experience on the Trainium3 TorchTitan and TorchNeuron stack, along with our experience of Trainium’s Neuron Explorer profiler, which is way better than both Nvidia’s and AMD’s profilers. We created a bunch of demos to show how Trainium’s profiler is “GPU Impossible.” In an upcoming article, we will go deep on writing speed-of-light NKI kernels and microbenchmarking on Trainium3. For our deep dive into the Trainium hardware, check out our previous article where we do a complete hardware breakdown. SemiAnalysis is hiring for various Member of Technical Staff roles. title: Serverless routing made sticky
summary: Voice agents, multiplayer games, and other workloads can now build on Sticky Sessions. Achieve strong affinity without losing autoscaling. Here’s how we built this on Modal Servers.
story_key: story|title:serverless routing made sticky
content_excerpt: At Modal, our serverless compute powers real-time inference, training, and batch jobs, scaling automatically with demand. Sandboxes offer a different model, containers whose lifecycles you explicitly control. A growing number of workloads require something in-between; autoscaling serverless compute that maintains continuity between requests. Consider a speech-to-text model with decoder state for an audio stream, a voice agent that holds a conversation, or a multiplayer game . For these workloads, users must come back to the same container on every reconnect for the entirety of their session. We recently launched Sticky Sessions , built on top of our low-latency Modal Servers . Every session’s requests land on the same container. To use Sticky Sessions, just create a Modal Server with the @modal.sessioned() decorator and start the sessions with the SDK or the HTTP API : Modal has supported WebSockets via Web Functions for some time. However, a WebSocket connection is tied to a Function “input”, not a container—if the connection drops, a new input is created on reconnect and can land on a different container. Stateful web UIs such as Gradio and Streamlit are workloads that need strong affinity guarantees between requests and backend containers. Every request has to reach the process that holds the user’s state. One anti-pattern workaround is setting max_containers=1 , which guarantees stickiness by giving up scaling entirely. Modal Servers already provide a softer form of affinity ; requests that share the same Modal-Affinity-Routing-Key header are routed to the same container in a best-effort manner. The container can still be scaled down or replaced at any time, routing future requests to a different container. Sticky Sessions provide stronger routing guarantees by ensuring all requests in the same session land on the same container. Sticky Sessions build on the infrastructure we developed for Modal Servers . At the core of this infrastructure is our in-house stateless proxy (fprs). The proxy provides low-latency routing and load balancing using in-memory cached routing state reconciled from durable storage. Servers already give us a way to route HTTP traffic to a container, manage container lifecycles, and scale the fleet based on demand. Sticky Sessions needed three things that the current request-level routing didn’t provide: From the client’s perspective, a Sticky Session works like a pipe. title: claude-code v2.1.309
summary:
What's changed

  • Fixed sandboxed Bash commands on macOS and Linux running the shell's startup files outside the sandbox before each command
  • Fixed macOS sandbox denyWrite glob patterns not applying at a path's real location when the pattern's folder is reached through a symlink
  • Fixed sandboxed commands and auto-accepted edits being able to modify the MCP config file passed with --mcp-config
  • Fixed a disabled MCP server being reconnected by a later permission prompt in print and SDK sessions
  • Fixed the Bash permission check trusting a variable set by a command whose redirect can fail to open
  • Fixed Bash permission checks not prompting for some compound commands that change directory before running git when the cd is wrapped or prefixed, as they do for a plain cd
  • Fixed an Edit(path) deny rule not blocking a Bash redirect to that path in some commands that also held a subshell
  • Fixed worktree-isolated sessions accepting some locale-prefixed commands the isolation guard should refuse
  • Fixed worktree-isolated sessions on zsh accepting some arithmetic commands that the isolation guard should refuse
  • Fixed worktrees and branch checkouts that Claude Code creates so they ignore git replace refs, as its other git operations already do
  • Fixed profile store write protection not applying when the config directory is reached through a symlink
  • Fixed sessions compacting repeatedly after reading files under a very large nested CLAUDE.md; a nested CLAUDE.md over the size limit now loads only its start
  • Fixed ctrl+enter (send now) only queuing a message when pressed before the response had started, and restarting a prompt's hooks while leaving the message queued when pressed while those hooks were running
  • Fixed key-bound slash commands running in the shell from ! mode
  • Fixed ctrl+o not showing messages from other agents and sessions that are still waiting to be delivered; they now appear in full under the transcript, marked as waiting
  • Fixed long tool output previews being cut through an emoji, leaving session transcripts that jq could not parse
  • Fixed Read reporting "File does not exist" for PDF page ranges in Linux sandboxes that share the parent's /proc
  • Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop-hosted session sometimes being lost when its connection refreshed
  • Fixed features missing from Claude Code sessions in the Claude desktop app when the terminal on the same computer was signed in to a different account or organization
  • Fixed the claude remote-control status line showing HEAD as the branch for a folder that is not in a git repository
  • Fixed split-pane agent teammates not inheriting the tool deny and --tools rules given on the leader's command line
  • Fixed sessions renamed with /rename appearing to other sessions under a generated name after a VS Code window reload or a non-interactive --resume
  • Fixed the /rewind list showing "No code changes" for a turn that changed checkpointed files through /code-review --fix, a subagent or a shell command
  • Fixed /privacy-settings showing an out-of-date "Help improve our AI models" value; it now also says when the setting can't be fetched
  • Fixed feedback saying "try again later" when your organization does not accept feedback; it now shows the server's reason and where to report a bug
  • Fixed oversized /feedback reports failing instead of being resent without the transcript
  • Fixed a skill in an --add-dir folder being unreachable when another skill already held its name; it is now offered as <folder>:<name>
  • Fixed /verify and /code-review not finding a nested package's own skill when its files were changed from the shell
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying that ant beta:worker poll --on-work passes trace context to the command
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill's C# tracing setup missing spans from the cloud platform clients
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying that API spans for requests to Claude Platform on AWS can't join the caller's trace
  • Fixed hooks that run in PowerShell not blocking when the hook's program exits with code 2, and on Windows PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks with "shell": "powershell" failing open when Git for Windows isn't installed
  • Fixed a mod's turn.step hook that names a model by alias, such as haiku, failing every request with a model error: the alias now resolves to its model
  • Fixed plugins and skills synced from claude.ai being removed, sometimes mid-session, after a disk read error
  • Fixed artifact publishes and updates being refused for some ordinary pages, such as pages with certain minified scripts or artifacts Claude could not read first
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission on each artifact update for the rest of a turn after the conversation was compacted in that turn
  • Fixed fine-grained tool streaming staying off on Amazon Bedrock when ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL is set to the default bedrock-runtime.<region>.amazonaws.com endpoint
  • Fixed the "Waiting for API response" hint flickering behind gateways that send only keepalive pings: routes off Anthropic's backend now wait 45 seconds
  • Fixed Claude notifying unrelated GitHub users by writing role names and placeholders as mentions in PRs, issues and comments
  • Linux: Fixed sandbox write denies lifting when a background command outlived the session
  • Windows: Fixed PowerShell permission checks auto-approving some Set-Location or cd commands that target the current directory and carry extra arguments; these now prompt for approval
  • macOS: Fixed the "Install Command Line Developer Tools" dialog opening each time Claude Code starts on a Mac without Xcode or the Command Line Tools
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --startup-timeout-min stopping a session whose first prompt, such as /code-review, was still working in a subagent; a frozen process is still stopped
  • Improved the speed of many git commands Claude Code runs for itself on Windows; on every platform, errors from those commands now show in English even when git is set to another language
  • Improved the error when a hooks module is nested too deep to load: it now names the file instead of showing a bare stack-overflow message
  • Improved disk-full handling: a Bash command cut off by a full disk now says so and names the folder to free up, and starting on a full temp volume prints a clear message, not a raw ENOSPC error
  • Improved the /claude-api skill to offer API tracing alongside SDK tracing when asked to add OpenTelemetry
  • Improved the /claude-api skill to check the live docs before saying a feature is unsupported
  • Self-hosted runner: Improved sessions that move to a new runner: Claude now sees the tool call that was interrupted, marked as outcome unknown
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to accept APCA as a text-contrast measure (keeping WCAG 2 ratios where AA conformance is required), add an apca(text, background) function to its palette validator scripts, and say whether a label inside a colored chart fill should be white or near-black
  • Updated the /claude-api skill: service account keys and Workload Identity Federation tokens can now manage OpenTelemetry destinations
  • Changed sed -i to get the standard Bash prompt and run as written, not a simulated file-edit preview; like other Bash edits, it is no longer restored by /rewind
  • Changed claude ultrareview to require workspace trust: it asks on a terminal, else refuses; scripts pass --trust-workspace, which takes no value (put a PR number or base branch before it), or set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRAREVIEW_TRUST_CHECK=1
  • Changed the dangerous rm and rmdir prompt in bypass permissions mode in the Desktop app and VS Code to deny the command at once with a rewrite hint, so unattended sessions keep going
  • Changed commands the settings exclude from the sandbox to ask before writing to its write-list paths while the sandbox is enabled but cannot run; the unsandboxed fallback is refused there
  • Changed worktree creation and reuse so git no longer fetches objects on demand, in ordinary clones and in partial clones with a Bash sandbox configured; such a partial clone fetches them first
  • Changed the /claude-api skill to build Managed Agents subagent teams on multiagent_20261001 with dynamic workflows on by default, instead of coordinator
  • [VSCode] Added a log warning that says what to do when dictation or the extension's own requests fail certificate verification, such as behind a TLS-inspecting proxy
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Claude panel staying blank after the editor cached an incomplete copy of its files; it now recovers by itself, or says what went wrong and how to fix it
  • [VSCode] Fixed Session history filling up with empty "Untitled" sessions each time you start a new session without sending a message
  • [VSCode] Fixed long slash-command messages such as /goal filling the chat panel; they now fold behind Show more like other prompts (#97469)
  • [VSCode] Fixed long messages not folding behind Show more after the chat panel is made narrower
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+J in the chat input always inserting a newline: it is now left to VS Code and the OS when "ctrl+j" is set to null in the Chat context of ~/.claude/keybindings.json
  • [VSCode] Fixed a mod's "From the … plugin" label above the prompt being drawn over the slash command and @-mention menus (#102981)
  • [VSCode] Fixed an empty list item, paragraph or code block, and list items renumbered from 1, when pasting copied LaTeX math
  • [VSCode] Fixed the feedback error showing only an HTTP status when your organization does not accept feedback
  • [VSCode] Improved Edit and Write speed in the chat panel: the wait for new problems after each edit is now 0.75 seconds in most cases, down from 1 to 1.5 seconds
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the Add connector list in routine forms saying no connectors were available while they were still loading
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the cloud environment editor shuffling environment variables and adding backslashes to values that contain both kinds of quote
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings so its title, tabs and buttons stay in view while only the content scrolls
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the "read documentation" tool row in cloud sessions, which showed escaped JSON instead of a readable page
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved a cloud session's Changes pane, which now says when it lists only pushed commits or only Claude's edits
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack posting a draft you approved for a channel into your DM by mistake; a post with no channel is now refused so it can go to the approved channel
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Allow and Deny on Claude's approval cards in Slack doing nothing when the session had stopped; your answer now restarts the session
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude ignoring untagged messages in a Slack channel after its workspace moved to a different Claude organization, including unshared channels on Enterprise Grid
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in a Slack channel posting a threaded reply before reading a newer message someone had just added to that thread
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Slack page in Claude Tag admin settings saying no workspaces were connected when the list failed to load; it now shows an error with a Retry button
  • [Code Review] Fixed a finished review showing no check on the pull request when earlier tries to create it failed; a final try now adds a completed check
  • [Code Review] Fixed a push queued behind a running review still starting a review after @claude review stop; its check now closes and says why
